blocks.html: Almost every number a computer produces is an approximation: a rounded constant, a truncated series, the last step of an iteration. Before we can compare methods we need a precise way to say how good an approximation is. You met the idea as Percent Error; here we sharpen it and connect it to scientific notation and significant digits.

Let $x$ be the true value and $\tilde{x}$ an approximation of it. The absolute error is $$|\tilde{x} - x|,$$ and, when $x \ne 0$, the relative error is $$\frac{|\tilde{x} - x|}{|x|}.$$ The absolute error carries the units of $x$. The relative error has no units; multiplied by 100 it is the percent error.

Absolute error measures the size of the mistake. Relative error measures it in units of the true value, so it says how many leading digits are right: a relative error near $10^{-t}$ means about $t$ correct significant digits.

Write $x = m \times 10^{e}$ with $1 \le |m| < 10$. If $\tilde{x}$ agrees with $x$ through the $t$-th significant digit, their difference is at most about half a unit in that place, $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 10^{e - t + 1}$. Dividing by $|x| \ge 10^{e}$ gives a relative error of at most $5 \times 10^{-t}$, whatever $e$ is. The size of the number cancels out; that is why relative error is the natural measure for numbers of any size, and why floating-point arithmetic is designed around it.

blocks.title: Both errors
blocks.q: A tank holds $x = 250$ L, and a gauge reads $\tilde{x} = 248$ L. Find the absolute and relative errors.
steps: Divide by the true value, $250$, not by the reading.

blocks.title: Comparing approximations of different sizes
blocks.q: Which is the better approximation: $3.14$ for $\pi$, or $384{,}000$ km for the average distance to the Moon, $384{,}400$ km?
steps: Absolute errors: $|3.14 - \pi| \approx 0.00159$ and $400$ km. The second looks enormous.
Measured relative to their size, $3.14$ is about twice as good, though both are right to about 3 significant digits.

blocks.title: Counting significant digits
blocks.q: How many significant digits does $\tilde{x} = 2.718$ have as an approximation of $e = 2.71828183\ldots$?
steps: It is at most $5 \times 10^{-4}$ but more than $5 \times 10^{-5}$, so $t = 4$, matching the 4 digits written.

blocks.html: Dividing by the approximation instead of the true value, or comparing absolute errors of numbers of very different sizes. An error of 400 km in the distance to the Moon is better, relatively, than an error of 1 m in the length of a room. Quick check: a relative error should not change when you change units (meters to centimeters); an absolute error does.
In practice the true value is unknown. Error bounds, estimates and comparisons between two approximations take its place, as later topics show.

blocks.html: Computers store numbers in base 2. Whole numbers convert easily, but fractions hold a surprise that explains why a computer cannot store $0.1$ exactly. The story is the same one you met with Repeating Decimals as Fractions, told in base 2, and it is the first step toward measuring the errors a computer makes.
After the binary point, the places are worth $\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4}, \frac{1}{8}, \frac{1}{16}, \ldots$ So $0.101_2 = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{8} = 0.625$.

To write a fraction $0 \le x < 1$ in base 2, double it: the whole-number part (0 or 1) is the next binary digit; keep the fraction part and repeat. A fraction in lowest terms ends in base 2 exactly when its denominator is a power of 2; otherwise its digits repeat forever.

If $x = 0.b_1b_2b_3\ldots_2$, then $2x = b_1.b_2b_3\ldots_2$: doubling moves the binary point one place right, so the whole part of $2x$ is $b_1$ and the fraction part holds the remaining digits. For $x = \frac{a}{n}$, every fraction part that appears has the form $\frac{r}{n}$ with $0 \le r < n$. There are only $n$ choices, so either some step gives $0$ (the expansion ends) or a fraction part comes back and the digits repeat from there. Ending means $x = \frac{k}{2^{j}}$, so in lowest terms the denominator must divide a power of 2.

steps: Check: $0.101_2 = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{8} = \frac{5}{8} = 0.625$. The denominator $8 = 2^{3}$, so three digits are enough.

blocks.html: Expecting every short decimal to have a short binary form. $0.5$, $0.25$ and $0.375$ end in binary, but $0.1$, $0.2$ and $0.3$ never do, so a computer must cut them off and round. Quick check: write the decimal as a fraction in lowest terms and look at the denominator. Any factor other than 2 (such as the 5 in 10) means the binary digits go on forever.
This is why $0.1 + 0.2$ is not exactly $0.3$ on a computer: none of the three is stored exactly. The next topic, Floating-Point Numbers, measures how far off they are.

blocks.html: A floating-point number is scientific notation in base 2 with a fixed number of digits. Because most fractions do not end in binary (see Binary Fractions), nearly every real number has to be rounded to fit, and the pattern of that rounding explains a lot of computer arithmetic.

A (normalized) float with $p$ fraction bits is $$x = \pm(1.b_1b_2\ldots b_p)_2 \times 2^{e},$$ where the exponent $e$ lies in a fixed range. A double (IEEE 754 double precision) uses 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits and $p = 52$ fraction bits: 64 bits in all, with 53 significant bits counting the leading 1, which is not stored.

Between $2^{e}$ and $2^{e+1}$ the floats are evenly spaced, $2^{e - p}$ apart, and the spacing doubles at each power of 2. Machine epsilon $\varepsilon = 2^{-p}$ is the gap between $1$ and the next float; for doubles $\varepsilon = 2^{-52} \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-16}$. Rounding to the nearest float has relative error at most $u = \varepsilon/2$.

Inside $[2^{e}, 2^{e+1})$ only the fraction bits change, and the last one is worth $2^{-p} \times 2^{e}$: that is the gap. For $x$ in that range the gap is at most $2^{-p} \cdot 2^{e} \le \varepsilon|x|$. Rounding to the nearest float moves $x$ by at most half a gap, so $$\frac{|\mathrm{fl}(x) - x|}{|x|} \le \frac{\varepsilon}{2} = u.$$ The absolute error grows with $|x|$, but the relative error never exceeds $u$: about 16 significant decimal digits for doubles.

blocks.html: Every stored number carries a tiny relative error, at most $u \approx 10^{-16}$ (see Floating-Point Numbers). Usually that is harmless. But subtracting two nearly equal numbers can turn tiny relative errors into a huge one. The cure is often algebra you already know, such as rationalizing with a conjugate (Adding and Multiplying Radicals).

When $a \approx b$, the leading digits of $a - b$ cancel, and the digits that remain come from the rounding errors of $a$ and $b$. Avoid the subtraction by rewriting the formula: $\sqrt{x + 1} - \sqrt{x} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x + 1} + \sqrt{x}}$.

Suppose $a$ and $b$ are stored with absolute errors $\delta_a$ and $\delta_b$, each at most $u|a|$. The subtraction itself is nearly exact, but its result inherits both errors: $$\frac{|(\tilde{a} - \tilde{b}) - (a - b)|}{|a - b|} \le \frac{u(|a| + |b|)}{|a - b|}.$$ The factor $\frac{|a| + |b|}{|a - b|}$ is huge when $a \approx b$. If $a$ and $b$ agree in their first $d$ digits, it is about $10^{d}$: roughly $d$ correct digits are lost.

blocks.q: Compute $\sqrt{1001} - \sqrt{1000}$, rounding every result to 4 significant digits.
steps: The true value is $0.015807\ldots$: the computed one has only 1 significant digit and is off by $27\%$.

blocks.title: Rewrite to avoid it
blocks.q: Compute the same quantity as $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1001} + \sqrt{1000}}$ in 4-digit arithmetic.
steps: All 4 digits are right. The same rounded roots went in; only the formula changed.

blocks.title: Cancellation in double precision
blocks.q: For $x = 10^{-8}$, a computer evaluates $1 - \cos x$ as $0$. What happened, and what is the fix?
steps: $\cos(10^{-8}) = 1 - 5 \times 10^{-17} + \cdots$, which is closer to $1$ than half the gap above or below $1$, so it is stored as exactly $1$.
Then $1 - 1 = 0$: every digit was lost, although the true value is about $5 \times 10^{-17}$.
Use $1 - \cos x = 2\sin^{2}\frac{x}{2}$: $2\sin^{2}(5 \times 10^{-9}) \approx 5 \times 10^{-17}$, correct to full precision.

items: $\sqrt{x + 1} - \sqrt{x} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x + 1} + \sqrt{x}}$ for large $x$.
$1 - \cos x = 2\sin^{2}(x/2)$ for small $x$.
$\ln(x + 1) - \ln x = \ln(1 + 1/x)$ for large $x$.
For small $x$, $e^{x} - 1 = x + \frac{x^{2}}{2} + \cdots$ (a library function expm1 does this).

blocks.html: Cancellation is not a bug in the subtraction: the computer subtracts the two stored numbers exactly. The damage was done earlier, when $a$ and $b$ were rounded; subtraction only exposes it.

Trusting every digit a computer prints. After cancellation the leading digits are gone, and most of what is printed is round-off. Quick check: if the two numbers you subtract agree in their first $d$ digits, expect to lose about $d$ of your roughly 16 digits.

blocks.html: Many numerical methods replace an infinite process with a finite one: a series is cut off, a limit $h \to 0$ is replaced by a small $h$, an integral by a sum. The error this causes is truncation error. It belongs to the method and would be there even with exact arithmetic; round-off error, from storing a limited number of digits, is a separate thing. You met the first kind of truncation error in Taylor's Inequality.

We describe truncation error by how fast it shrinks with a step size $h$. The error $E(h)$ is of order $h^{p}$, written $E(h) = O(h^{p})$, when $|E(h)| \le Ch^{p}$ for some constant $C$ and all small enough $h$. The larger $p$, the faster the method improves as $h$ shrinks.
If $E(h) \approx Ch^{p}$, halving $h$ divides the error by about $2^{p}$. Conversely, from the errors at $h$ and $h/2$ you can read off the order: $p \approx \log_2\frac{E(h)}{E(h/2)}$.

Taylor's theorem shows where the power comes from. For example, $$f(x + h) = f(x) + hf'(x) + \frac{h^{2}}{2}f''(\xi)$$ for some $\xi$ between $x$ and $x + h$, so $$\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} - f'(x) = \frac{h}{2}f''(\xi).$$ The truncation error is $O(h)$: as $h \to 0$, the leading term $\frac{h}{2}f''(x)$ dominates everything after it, so $E(h) \approx Ch$ with $C = \frac{1}{2}f''(x)$. A log–log plot of error against $h$ is then a straight line of slope $p$.

Bound: $\frac{1.2 \times 0.001}{6} = 0.0002$. The actual error is $e^{0.1} - 1.105 = 0.000171\ldots$, inside the bound.

blocks.title: Predicting the error
blocks.q: A method of order 4 has error $3.2 \times 10^{-5}$ with $h = 0.2$. Estimate the error with $h = 0.1$, and the $h$ needed for $10^{-9}$.
steps: For $10^{-9}$ the error must shrink by $3.2 \times 10^{4}$ from $h = 0.2$, so $h$ must shrink by $(3.2 \times 10^{4})^{1/4} \approx 13.4$: $h \approx 0.015$.

blocks.html: Mixing up truncation error with round-off error. Truncation error comes from the method (a cut-off series, a finite $h$) and shrinks as you take more terms or smaller steps. Round-off comes from storing about 16 digits and does not depend on the method's formula. Test: would the error vanish with infinitely many digits? If not, it is truncation error.

blocks.html: Inputs are never exact: they are measured, or rounded to doubles. So we must ask how much a small change in the input can change the answer. That is a property of the problem, before any method enters. The tool is the Linear Approximation and Differentials, and the bad case is the one you met in Round-Off and Cancellation.

For a function $f$ of one variable, the condition number at $x$ is $$\kappa(x) = \left|\frac{xf'(x)}{f(x)}\right|.$$ A problem is well-conditioned when $\kappa$ is modest and ill-conditioned when $\kappa$ is large.

A relative change $\delta$ in the input changes the output by a relative amount of about $\kappa\delta$. With input errors near $10^{-16}$, an answer can only be trusted to about $16 - \log_{10}\kappa$ digits, whatever method computes it.

Change $x$ by a relative amount $\delta$, to $x(1 + \delta)$. By linear approximation, $f(x + x\delta) \approx f(x) + f'(x)x\delta$. So the relative change in the output is $$\frac{f(x + x\delta) - f(x)}{f(x)} \approx \frac{xf'(x)}{f(x)}\delta.$$ The factor in front of $\delta$ is the condition number (up to sign). It compares relative changes, so it does not depend on units or on the size of $x$.

blocks.title: A well-conditioned problem
blocks.q: Find $\kappa$ for $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$.
steps: $\kappa = \frac{1}{2}$ everywhere: a square root halves relative errors.

blocks.title: Subtraction is ill-conditioned
blocks.q: Find $\kappa$ for $f(x) = x - 1$ at $x = 1.001$, and the effect of an input error of $10^{-16}$.
steps: A relative input error of $10^{-16}$ becomes about $1001 \times 10^{-16} \approx 10^{-13}$ in the output: about 3 digits lost.
This is cancellation seen as a property of the problem: no formula for $x - 1$ can avoid it once $x$ itself is uncertain.

blocks.html: The same idea works for any problem: compare the relative change in the answer with the relative change in the data that caused it. For a linear system $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ that ratio is bounded by the condition number of the matrix, which plays exactly this role later in the course.

blocks.html: Conditioning tells us how sensitive a problem is. Now the other half: does an algorithm add more error than the problem forces? Two formulas that are equal in exact arithmetic can behave very differently in floating point.

An algorithm $\tilde{f}$ for $f$ is backward stable if for every input $x$, $$\tilde{f}(x) = f(\tilde{x})\quad\text{for some } \tilde{x} \text{ with } \frac{|\tilde{x} - x|}{|x|} = O(u).$$ In words: the computed answer is the exact answer to a slightly changed question. An algorithm that magnifies its own rounding errors far beyond that is unstable.

Accuracy depends on both: for a backward stable algorithm, relative error $\approx \kappa \cdot u$. A stable method on a well-conditioned problem gives an accurate answer; an unstable method can fail even on an easy problem; and no method beats an ill-conditioned problem.

If $\tilde{f}(x) = f(\tilde{x})$ with $\tilde{x} = x(1 + \delta)$ and $|\delta| \approx u$, then by the definition of the condition number $$\frac{|\tilde{f}(x) - f(x)|}{|f(x)|} = \frac{|f(\tilde{x}) - f(x)|}{|f(x)|} \approx \kappa|\delta| \approx \kappa u.$$ So the error splits into two factors: $u$, which a stable algorithm keeps small, and $\kappa$, which belongs to the problem.

blocks.title: Same formula, two algorithms
blocks.q: The small root of $x^{2} - 200x + 1 = 0$ is $0.00500012\ldots$ Compute it in 4-digit arithmetic with $\frac{200 - \sqrt{200^{2} - 4}}{2}$ and with $\frac{2}{200 + \sqrt{200^{2} - 4}}$.
steps: First formula: $\frac{200 - 200.0}{2} = 0$. Every digit is lost to cancellation.
Second formula (the first times the conjugate over itself): $\frac{2}{400.0} = 0.005000$, right to all 4 digits.
The root itself is well-conditioned; the first formula is unstable for it, the second is stable.

blocks.title: An unstable recurrence
blocks.q: $I_n = \int_0^1 x^{n}e^{x - 1}\,dx$ satisfies $I_n = 1 - nI_{n-1}$ with $I_0 = 1 - e^{-1}$. If $I_0$ is stored with error $10^{-16}$, how large is the error in $I_{20}$?
steps: An error $\epsilon$ in $I_{n-1}$ becomes $n\epsilon$ in size in $I_n$, so after 20 steps the error is $20!\,\epsilon$.
But $0 < I_{20} < \frac{1}{21}$: the computed value is garbage. Running the recurrence backward, $I_{n-1} = \frac{1 - I_n}{n}$, divides errors by $n$ each step: stable.

blocks.title: A stable method on a hard problem
blocks.q: A backward stable solver is used on a problem with $\kappa \approx 10^{10}$. How many digits can we expect?
steps: About 6 correct digits: the method did its job; the problem allows no more.

blocks.html: Thinking a stable algorithm always gives an accurate answer. Stability promises only a small backward error; on an ill-conditioned problem that still means a large error in the answer. Check both: estimate $\kappa$ for the problem, and ask whether the algorithm subtracts nearly equal numbers or multiplies errors step after step.

blocks.html: Evaluating a polynomial looks too simple to need an algorithm, but the obvious way wastes work. Synthetic division already contains a better way: the remainder of dividing $p(x)$ by $x - c$ is $p(c)$, and the steps of synthetic division are exactly Horner's method.

Factor $x$ out again and again: $$a_3x^{3} + a_2x^{2} + a_1x + a_0 = ((a_3x + a_2)x + a_1)x + a_0.$$ Start with $b = a_n$, then for $k = n - 1$ down to $0$ replace $b$ by $bx + a_k$. The last $b$ is $p(x)$.
Horner's method evaluates a degree-$n$ polynomial with only $n$ multiplications and $n$ additions, starting from the leading coefficient and writing a $0$ for every missing power.

Term by term, $a_kx^{k}$ costs $k$ multiplications if each power is built from scratch: $1 + 2 + \cdots + n = \frac{n(n + 1)}{2}$ in all. Even reusing powers costs about $2n$. The nested form does one multiply and one add per coefficient. Fewer operations also means fewer roundings, and the intermediate values $b$ have a meaning of their own: they are the coefficients of the quotient $q(x)$ in $p(x) = (x - c)q(x) + p(c)$.

blocks.html: In code the whole method is two lines: set b = a[n], then for k = n - 1 down to 0 set b = b*x + a[k]. Each pass through the loop does one rounding in the multiply and one in the add, so the computed value is close to the exact value of a polynomial whose coefficients have been changed only slightly: Horner's method is backward stable.

Starting the nesting from the constant term, or skipping a missing power instead of writing a $0$ for it. Both evaluate the wrong polynomial. Check: the number of steps must equal the degree, and a quick direct evaluation at $x = 1$ (the sum of the coefficients) should match.
Horner's method is the standard way to evaluate polynomials in software; it is also the inner loop of Newton's method for polynomials, where $p(c)$ and $p'(c)$ come from two passes.

blocks.html: The The Intermediate Value Theorem promises a root of a continuous $f$ wherever $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ have opposite signs. Bisection turns that promise into an algorithm: keep cutting the interval in half, always keeping the half where the sign changes.

items: Start with $[a, b]$ where $f$ is continuous and $f(a)f(b) < 0$.
Compute the midpoint $m = \frac{a + b}{2}$ and $f(m)$. If $f(m) = 0$, stop.
If $f(m)$ has the same sign as $f(a)$, replace $a$ by $m$; otherwise replace $b$ by $m$.
Repeat until the interval is as short as you need.

blocks.html: After $n$ halvings the interval has width $\frac{b - a}{2^{n}}$, so its midpoint is within $\frac{b - a}{2^{n+1}}$ of a root. Bisection gains one binary digit per step, about one decimal digit every 3.3 steps, and it cannot fail when its conditions hold.

At every step the endpoints still have opposite signs, so by the Intermediate Value Theorem a root stays inside the interval. The interval is halved each time, and any point of an interval is within half its width of its midpoint. The error bound therefore halves every step: linear convergence with ratio $\frac{1}{2}$. Since $\log_{10}2 \approx 0.301$, it takes about $1/0.301 \approx 3.3$ steps for each new decimal digit.

blocks.html: Many root-finding methods have the same shape: rewrite $f(x) = 0$ as $x = g(x)$, pick $x_0$, and repeat $$x_{n+1} = g(x_n).$$ If the iterates settle at a value $r$ and $g$ is continuous, then $r = g(r)$: a fixed point of $g$, and so a root of $f$. Whether they settle is decided by the The Mean Value Theorem and the derivative $g'$.

Near a fixed point $r$, each step multiplies the error by about $g'(r)$. The iteration converges from nearby starting points when $|g'(r)| < 1$ (linearly, with ratio $|g'(r)|$) and moves away when $|g'(r)| > 1$.

Subtract $r = g(r)$ from $x_{n+1} = g(x_n)$ and use the Mean Value Theorem: $$x_{n+1} - r = g(x_n) - g(r) = g'(\xi_n)(x_n - r)$$ for some $\xi_n$ between $x_n$ and $r$. If $|g'| \le L < 1$ on an interval around $r$ that holds $x_0$, every step keeps the iterate in that interval and shrinks the error by at least $L$: $|x_n - r| \le L^{n}|x_0 - r| \to 0$. If $|g'(r)| > 1$, the same equation shows errors growing.

blocks.html: The Bisection Method halves its error every step; the good rearrangement in Fixed-Point Iteration seemed to double its correct digits. "Order of convergence" makes this difference precise. With $e_n = |x_n - r|$, a method has order $p$ if $$e_{n+1} \approx Ce_n^{p}$$ for large $n$, with a constant $C > 0$ (and $C < 1$ when $p = 1$).

Order 1 (linear): each step gains the same number of digits, $\log_{10}\frac{1}{C}$. Order 2 (quadratic): the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step. To estimate $p$ from three errors use logarithms: $$p \approx \frac{\ln(e_{n+1}/e_n)}{\ln(e_n/e_{n-1})}.$$

Take $-\log_{10}$ of $e_{n+1} \approx Ce_n^{p}$. With $d_n = -\log_{10}e_n$ (roughly the number of correct digits), $$d_{n+1} \approx p\,d_n - \log_{10}C.$$ For $p = 1$ the digits grow by a fixed amount; for $p = 2$ they double. For the estimate, divide $e_{n+1} \approx Ce_n^{p}$ by $e_n \approx Ce_{n-1}^{p}$: $\frac{e_{n+1}}{e_n} \approx \left(\frac{e_n}{e_{n-1}}\right)^{p}$, and the power rule for logarithms brings $p$ down.

blocks.html: Between the two extremes is superlinear convergence: the ratio $\frac{e_{n+1}}{e_n}$ goes to $0$, so the method speeds up as it goes, but the order may be less than 2. The secant method, with order about $1.618$, is the standard example. Higher order is not everything, though: what matters in practice is the work per digit gained, which also depends on how much each step costs.

In real problems the root $r$ is unknown, so $e_n$ is too. Near convergence the change between iterates, $|x_{n+1} - x_n|$, is a good stand-in for $e_n$ when the method is faster than linear, and it is the usual stopping test: stop when it falls below the tolerance you need.

Estimating the order from the ratio $\frac{e_{n+1}}{e_n}$ alone. For any order above 1 that ratio goes to $0$, so it cannot tell order 2 from order 3; it only separates linear from faster. The order comes from logarithms, as in the formula above, or from checking which ratio $\frac{e_{n+1}}{e_n^{p}}$ settles to a constant.

blocks.html: You know Newton's Method: $x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}$. Using the language of order of convergence, we can now say exactly how fast it is near a root, and why it sometimes fails.

Near a simple root $r$ (one with $f'(r) \ne 0$), Newton's method converges quadratically: $$e_{n+1} \approx \left|\frac{f''(r)}{2f'(r)}\right|e_n^{2}.$$ Far from a root it can wander, cycle or blow up, and at a multiple root it slows to linear convergence.

Expand $f$ about $x_n$ and evaluate at the root: $0 = f(r) = f(x_n) + f'(x_n)(r - x_n) + \frac{f''(\xi)}{2}(r - x_n)^{2}$. Divide by $f'(x_n)$ and use $x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}$: $$x_{n+1} - r = \frac{f''(\xi)}{2f'(x_n)}(x_n - r)^{2}.$$ The square is the quadratic convergence. The derivation needs $f'(x_n)$ away from $0$ and $x_n$ close enough to $r$ that the error term is small.

blocks.html: The local promise matters: quadratic convergence starts only once the error is small enough that $Ce_n < 1$. Before that, Newton's method can behave in many ways. The common failures:

items: A start near a point where $f'(x) \approx 0$: the nearly flat tangent throws the next iterate far away.
A start in the wrong basin: the iterates may cycle or head to a different root.
A multiple root: convergence slows to linear.
A function like $\arctan x$: from $|x_0| \gtrsim 1.39$ the iterates grow in size and diverge.

blocks.html: Assuming Newton's method always converges. Its fast convergence is a local promise: only from a good enough start near a simple root. In practice, check that $|f(x_n)|$ decreases, cap the number of steps, and fall back to a safe method such as The Bisection Method when it does not.

blocks.html: Newton's method needs the derivative $f'$, which may be costly or unavailable. The secant method replaces the tangent with the line through the two most recent points: $$x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)\frac{x_n - x_{n-1}}{f(x_n) - f(x_{n-1})}.$$

The secant method needs two starting values, uses one new function value per step and no derivative, and near a simple root converges with order $\frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2} \approx 1.618$. Each step uses the two newest points, whether or not they bracket the root.

The fraction is $1/(\text{slope of the secant line})$, a difference quotient standing in for $f'(x_n)$. A Taylor argument like Newton's gives $e_{n+1} \approx Ce_ne_{n-1}$: the error is the product of the last two errors. If $e_{n+1} \approx Ke_n^{p}$, substituting into that relation forces $p^{2} = p + 1$, whose positive root is the golden ratio $1.618\ldots$. Per evaluation of $f$, this beats Newton's method whenever $f'$ costs about as much as $f$: two Newton evaluations give order 2, so one gives order $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$.

blocks.html: To solve several equations in several unknowns, $\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}$, Newton's idea carries over: replace $\mathbf{F}$ by its linear approximation and solve that. The derivative becomes a matrix of Partial Derivatives, and dividing by it becomes solving a linear system, which you know from Inverses by Gauss–Jordan. Its convergence matches Newton's method in one variable.
For $\mathbf{F} = (F_1, \ldots, F_n)$, the Jacobian $J(\mathbf{x})$ is the $n \times n$ matrix with $$J_{ij} = \frac{\partial F_i}{\partial x_j}:$$ row $i$ holds the partial derivatives of $F_i$.

Newton's method for systems: solve $$J(\mathbf{x}_k)\,\boldsymbol{\Delta} = -\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}_k),$$ then set $\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{x}_k + \boldsymbol{\Delta}$. Near a root where $J$ is invertible it converges quadratically.

Linearize: $\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}_k + \boldsymbol{\Delta}) \approx \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}_k) + J(\mathbf{x}_k)\boldsymbol{\Delta}$. Setting the right side to $\mathbf{0}$ gives the linear system for the step. Writing $\boldsymbol{\Delta} = -J^{-1}\mathbf{F}$ shows the analogy with $-\frac{f}{f'}$, but in practice one solves the system by elimination; forming $J^{-1}$ costs more and is less accurate.

Building $J$ takes $n^{2}$ partial derivatives, and solving the linear system by elimination takes about $\frac{2}{3}n^{3}$ operations (see The Cost of Elimination). For large systems, methods that update an approximate Jacobian instead of recomputing it (quasi-Newton methods) are common.

Putting the partial derivatives in the wrong places, or forgetting the minus sign. Row $i$ of $J$ holds $\frac{\partial F_i}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial F_i}{\partial y}, \ldots$; the system is $J\boldsymbol{\Delta} = -\mathbf{F}$. Check: if $\mathbf{F}$ were linear, $\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}$, one Newton step from anywhere must land exactly on the solution.

blocks.html: You can solve a system by reducing it to Gaussian Elimination and Echelon Form and back substituting. On a computer the question becomes: how much work is that? We count flops (floating-point operations): each addition, subtraction, multiplication or division counts as one.

Gaussian elimination on an $n \times n$ matrix takes about $\frac{2}{3}n^{3}$ flops; each triangular solve (forward or back substitution) takes about $n^{2}$. Doubling $n$ multiplies the elimination work by about $2^{3} = 8$.

At step $k$, each of the $n - k$ rows below the pivot gets a multiplier (one division) and then has $n - k$ entries updated, each with a multiply and a subtract: about $2(n - k)^{2}$ flops for the step. Adding up, $$\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}2(n - k)^{2} = 2\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}j^{2} \approx \frac{2}{3}n^{3}.$$ In back substitution, the row $i$ places from the bottom needs $i - 1$ multiplies, $i - 1$ subtracts and one divide: $\sum_{i=1}^{n}(2i - 1) = n^{2}$.

blocks.html: By hand you swap rows only when a pivot is $0$. In floating point that is not enough: a pivot that is merely tiny produces huge multipliers, and the huge numbers swamp the information in the other rows. It is Round-Off and Cancellation again, this time inside elimination.

Partial pivoting: before eliminating in column $k$, find the row at or below the diagonal whose entry in column $k$ is largest in absolute value, and swap it into the pivot position. Then every multiplier satisfies $|m| \le 1$.

With pivot $\epsilon$ and multiplier $m = a_{21}/\epsilon$, the update $a_{22} - m\,a_{12}$ is dominated by $-m\,a_{12}$ when $|m|$ is huge. After rounding, the original $a_{22}$ (and the matching entry of $\mathbf{b}$) may vanish completely: the computer is now solving a different system. Choosing the largest available pivot keeps $|m| \le 1$, so no row is ever multiplied up before it is added to another, and entries cannot grow much from one step to the next. With partial pivoting, elimination is backward stable for practically every matrix met in practice.

Then $x = \frac{1 - 1.00}{10^{-4}} = 0$. Completely wrong: the 1 and the 2 in row 2 were rounded away.
Swap first: the multiplier is $10^{-4}$. Row 2 becomes $(1 - 10^{-4})y = 1 - 2 \times 10^{-4}$, which rounds to $1.00y = 1.00$: $y = 1.00$, and $x = 2 - 1.00 = 1.00$. Right to 3 digits.

Multipliers: $\frac{2}{-6} = -\frac{1}{3}$ and $\frac{4}{-6} = -\frac{2}{3}$, both at most 1 in size.
Eliminate: the new rows 2 and 3 are $(0, 2, -\frac{1}{3})$ and $(0, 0, \frac{19}{3})$.
Column 2 below the diagonal: $|2|$ and $|0|$, so no further swap is needed.

blocks.html: Swapping rows only when a pivot is exactly $0$. In floating point a pivot of $10^{-20}$ does just as much damage as $0$ does by hand, only silently: no division by zero warns you. Compare sizes with absolute values ($-6$ beats $4$), and swap whenever a larger entry sits below.
The row swaps are recorded in a permutation matrix $P$, giving the factorization $PA = LU$; the next topic, Solving with PA = LU, shows how to use it.

blocks.html: Elementary Matrices and LU Factorization records elimination as $A = LU$. With Partial Pivoting the rows get swapped along the way; a permutation matrix $P$ (the identity with its rows reordered) records the swaps, and the factorization becomes $$PA = LU,$$ with $L$ unit lower triangular (its multipliers all at most 1 in size) and $U$ upper triangular.

To solve $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ from $PA = LU$: reorder $\mathbf{b}$ to $P\mathbf{b}$, solve $L\mathbf{y} = P\mathbf{b}$ by forward substitution, then $U\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}$ by back substitution. Factoring costs $\frac{2}{3}n^{3}$ flops once; each new $\mathbf{b}$ costs only $2n^{2}$.

Multiply $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ by $P$: $PA\mathbf{x} = P\mathbf{b}$, that is, $L(U\mathbf{x}) = P\mathbf{b}$. Call $U\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}$. Then $L\mathbf{y} = P\mathbf{b}$ is a lower triangular system, solved from the top down, and $U\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}$ is upper triangular, solved from the bottom up. Both are cheap because each unknown comes from one division once the earlier ones are known.

blocks.html: This split into "factor" and "solve" is how numerical libraries are organized, and it pays off whenever the same matrix meets many right-hand sides: Inverse and Shifted Power Methods solves with the same shifted matrix every step, implicit ODE methods with a fixed step solve with the same matrix every step, and the spline and boundary value systems later in the course are factored once and reused.

Reading $P$ is easy: row $i$ of $P$ has a single $1$, in column $j$, which means "entry $i$ of $P\mathbf{b}$ is entry $j$ of $\mathbf{b}$." Software usually stores $P$ as a list of row indices rather than as a matrix. In the example above, $P$ moves row 2 to the top, so $P\mathbf{b}$ starts with $b_2$.

Forgetting to apply the row swaps to $\mathbf{b}$ before forward substitution. $L$ and $U$ describe the swapped rows, so using $\mathbf{b}$ in its original order solves a different system. Check: multiply your answer by $A$; it must give back the original $\mathbf{b}$.
The same factors give $\det A = \pm u_{11}u_{22}\cdots u_{nn}$ (the sign set by the number of swaps), far cheaper than cofactor expansion.

blocks.html: To talk about the size of an error in a vector answer, we need the size of a vector. The length from the dot product, $\sqrt{\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{x}}$, is one choice; numerical work also uses two others that are cheaper and often easier to bound.

For $\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)$: $$\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert_1 = \sum|x_i|,\quad \lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum x_i^{2}},\quad \lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert_\infty = \max|x_i|.$$ Each is a norm: positive for $\mathbf{x} \ne \mathbf{0}$, scaled by $|c|$ when $\mathbf{x}$ is multiplied by $c$, and obeying the triangle inequality $\lVert\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}\rVert \le \lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert + \lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert$.

A matrix norm measures how much $A$ can stretch a vector: $$\lVert A\rVert = \max_{\mathbf{x} \ne \mathbf{0}}\frac{\lVert A\mathbf{x}\rVert}{\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert}.$$ So $\lVert A\mathbf{x}\rVert \le \lVert A\rVert\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert$ always.
$\lVert A\rVert_\infty$ is the largest absolute row sum and $\lVert A\rVert_1$ is the largest absolute column sum. ($\lVert A\rVert_2$ is the largest singular value, harder to compute by hand.)

Entry $i$ of $A\mathbf{x}$ is $\sum_j a_{ij}x_j$, so $|(A\mathbf{x})_i| \le \sum_j|a_{ij}|\,|x_j| \le \left(\sum_j|a_{ij}|\right)\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert_\infty$. The largest row sum therefore bounds the stretch, and choosing $x_j = \pm 1$ to match the signs in that row achieves it. For $\lVert\cdot\rVert_1$, $A\mathbf{x}$ is a combination of the columns of $A$, and the best one can do with $\sum|x_j| = 1$ is to put all the weight on the column with the largest absolute sum.

The vector $\mathbf{x} = (1, 1)$ matches the signs of row 2: $A\mathbf{x} = (-1, 7)$, and $\lVert A\mathbf{x}\rVert_\infty = 7 = 7 \cdot \lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert_\infty$. The bound is reached.

blocks.html: Why keep three norms? In $n$ dimensions they never differ by more than a fixed factor: for example $\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert_\infty \le \lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert_2 \le \sqrt{n}\,\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert_\infty$. So "the error goes to zero" means the same thing in all of them, and we pick whichever is easiest to compute or to bound. The $\infty$-norm answers "how wrong is the worst entry?", which is often what we want to know. Errors in a vector answer are then measured as $\frac{\lVert\tilde{\mathbf{x}} - \mathbf{x}\rVert}{\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert}$, just like relative error for numbers.

blocks.html: For a single function, Conditioning of a Problem measured how input errors grow. For $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ the same role is played by one number built from Vector and Matrix Norms and the inverse: $$\kappa(A) = \lVert A\rVert\,\lVert A^{-1}\rVert,$$ with the norm named when it matters, as in $\kappa_\infty(A)$. Always $\kappa(A) \ge 1$.

If $\mathbf{b}$ changes by $\delta\mathbf{b}$, the solution changes by $\delta\mathbf{x}$ with $$\frac{\lVert\delta\mathbf{x}\rVert}{\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert} \le \kappa(A)\frac{\lVert\delta\mathbf{b}\rVert}{\lVert\mathbf{b}\rVert}.$$ The same bound links a residual $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{b} - A\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$ to the error in $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$: a tiny residual can hide a large error when $\kappa$ is large. Roughly, $\log_{10}\kappa$ digits are lost.

From $A(\mathbf{x} + \delta\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{b} + \delta\mathbf{b}$ we get $A\,\delta\mathbf{x} = \delta\mathbf{b}$, so $\lVert\delta\mathbf{x}\rVert \le \lVert A^{-1}\rVert\lVert\delta\mathbf{b}\rVert$. Also $\lVert\mathbf{b}\rVert = \lVert A\mathbf{x}\rVert \le \lVert A\rVert\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert$, so $\frac{1}{\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert} \le \frac{\lVert A\rVert}{\lVert\mathbf{b}\rVert}$. Multiply the two inequalities. For the residual, $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$ solves $A\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{r}$ exactly, so $\delta\mathbf{b} = -\mathbf{r}$.

steps: $A\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = (2, 2)$, so the residual is $\mathbf{r} = (0, 0.01)$: relative size $\frac{0.01}{2.01} \approx 0.005$.

blocks.title: Digits to expect
blocks.q: The $10 \times 10$ Hilbert matrix, $h_{ij} = \frac{1}{i + j - 1}$, has $\kappa_2 \approx 1.6 \times 10^{13}$. About how many correct digits should we expect when solving with it in double precision?
steps: Data errors near $10^{-16}$ can grow by $\kappa$: relative error up to about $1.6 \times 10^{13} \times 10^{-16} \approx 2 \times 10^{-3}$.
So only about 3 correct digits, even with a stable method like elimination with partial pivoting.

blocks.html: Computing $A^{-1}$ just to find $\kappa$ would cost more than solving the system, so libraries estimate $\kappa_1(A)$ cheaply from the $LU$ factors and report it next to the answer. A few values to keep in mind: $\kappa = 1$ for the identity and, in the 2-norm, for every orthogonal matrix; $\kappa = \infty$ for a singular matrix; and a rough rule that a computed solution has about $16 - \log_{10}\kappa$ correct digits.

Trusting a solution because its residual $\mathbf{b} - A\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$ is tiny. That only says $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$ nearly satisfies the equations; if $\kappa(A)$ is large, nearly satisfying them is compatible with a large error. Another trap: a small determinant does not mean ill-conditioned ($0.1I$ has determinant $10^{-n}$ but $\kappa = 1$). Check $\kappa$, not $\det$.

blocks.html: For a large system with mostly zero entries, elimination's $\frac{2}{3}n^{3}$ flops (see The Cost of Elimination) can be far too many. An iterative method starts from a guess and improves it using only cheap products with $A$. Jacobi's method is the simplest, and it is a Fixed-Point Iteration in disguise.

Solve equation $i$ for $x_i$, and put the previous values on the right: $$x_i^{(k+1)} = \frac{1}{a_{ii}}\left(b_i - \sum_{j \ne i}a_{ij}x_j^{(k)}\right).$$ In matrix form, with $A = D + L + U$ (diagonal, strictly lower, strictly upper parts), $\mathbf{x}^{(k+1)} = D^{-1}\big(\mathbf{b} - (L + U)\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\big)$.

Jacobi updates every variable at once from the previous sweep. It converges from any start when $A$ is strictly diagonally dominant by rows: $|a_{ii}| > \sum_{j \ne i}|a_{ij}|$ in every row. The error shrinks by about the spectral radius $\rho(T)$ of $T = -D^{-1}(L + U)$ per sweep.

The exact solution satisfies the same formula, so subtracting gives $\mathbf{e}^{(k+1)} = T\mathbf{e}^{(k)}$ for the error. Row $i$ of $T$ has absolute sum $\sum_{j \ne i}\frac{|a_{ij}|}{|a_{ii}|}$, which is less than 1 for every row exactly when $A$ is strictly diagonally dominant. Then $\lVert T\rVert_\infty < 1$ and $\lVert\mathbf{e}^{(k)}\rVert_\infty \le \lVert T\rVert_\infty^{k}\lVert\mathbf{e}^{(0)}\rVert_\infty \to 0$, just as $|g'| < 1$ made fixed-point iteration converge.

blocks.title: Three sweeps
blocks.q: Apply Jacobi to $4x + y = 6$, $2x + 5y = 9$ from $(0, 0)$. (The solution is $(\frac{7}{6}, \frac{4}{3}) \approx (1.167, 1.333)$.)
steps: Iteration: $x \leftarrow \frac{6 - y}{4}$, $y \leftarrow \frac{9 - 2x}{5}$, both from the old values.
Sweep 3: $(\frac{6 - 1.2}{4}, \frac{9 - 2.1}{5}) = (1.2, 1.38)$, closing in on the solution from both sides.

blocks.html: One sweep costs about two flops per nonzero entry of $A$, so for a sparse matrix with a few nonzeros per row a sweep is cheap, far cheaper than elimination. In practice the iteration stops when the residual $\lVert\mathbf{b} - A\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\rVert$ is small compared with $\lVert\mathbf{b}\rVert$, or when successive iterates barely change. Diagonal dominance is enough for convergence but not necessary; what matters exactly is whether $\rho(T) < 1$.

Running the iteration on the equations as given, even when another order would make the system diagonally dominant. Before iterating, put each equation where its largest coefficient (in size) lands on the diagonal. Reordering equations never changes the solution, but it can turn a diverging iteration into a converging one.

blocks.html: In Jacobi's method, the new $x$ is already known when the new $y$ is computed, yet Jacobi ignores it. Gauss–Seidel uses each new value as soon as it exists: $$x_i^{(k+1)} = \frac{1}{a_{ii}}\left(b_i - \sum_{j < i}a_{ij}x_j^{(k+1)} - \sum_{j > i}a_{ij}x_j^{(k)}\right).$$ In matrix form, $(D + L)\mathbf{x}^{(k+1)} = \mathbf{b} - U\mathbf{x}^{(k)}$.

Gauss–Seidel updates the variables one at a time, always with the newest values. For strictly diagonally dominant matrices it converges, usually faster than Jacobi, and it needs only one copy of $\mathbf{x}$ in memory.

Fresh values are closer to the solution, so using them at once can only help when the iteration is converging. For a $2 \times 2$ system the effect is exact: the Gauss–Seidel iteration matrix has eigenvalues $0$ and $\frac{a_{12}a_{21}}{a_{11}a_{22}}$, while Jacobi's are $\pm\sqrt{\frac{a_{12}a_{21}}{a_{11}a_{22}}}$. So $\rho_{GS} = \rho_J^{2}$: one Gauss–Seidel sweep does as much as two Jacobi sweeps. (For many larger matrices from differential equations the same relation holds.)

blocks.title: Spot the method

steps: The $y$ update uses x_old, the value from the previous sweep.
That is Jacobi's method. Gauss–Seidel would use x_new in the $y$ update.

blocks.html: Keeping last sweep's values for variables that were already updated in this sweep. That is Jacobi's method, not Gauss–Seidel. Check each formula: every variable that comes earlier in the order must appear with its new value.

Strict diagonal dominance is one guarantee; another is that $A$ is symmetric with positive eigenvalues (symmetric positive definite), which is common in physics and engineering problems. In both cases Gauss–Seidel converges from any starting vector. A small change, multiplying each update by a factor $\omega$ between 1 and 2 (successive over-relaxation), can speed it up a great deal more.

Because Gauss–Seidel uses new values as it goes, its result depends on the order of the variables, and it is harder to run in parallel than Jacobi. Both are the starting points for faster methods such as successive over-relaxation and the Krylov methods used for very large systems.

blocks.html: In Writing Quadratics from Points you found the parabola through three points by solving three equations. Interpolation asks the same question for any number of points, and Lagrange's idea answers it with no system to solve, by building the polynomial from pieces that each vanish where they should, as in Writing a Polynomial from Its Zeros.

Given $n + 1$ points $(x_0, y_0), \ldots, (x_n, y_n)$ with different $x$-values (the nodes), define for each $k$ the Lagrange basis polynomial $$L_k(x) = \prod_{j \ne k}\frac{x - x_j}{x_k - x_j}.$$ Then the interpolating polynomial is $$p(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n}y_kL_k(x).$$

Exactly one polynomial of degree at most $n$ passes through $n + 1$ points with different $x$-values. Each $L_k$ is $1$ at its own node $x_k$ and $0$ at every other node, so $\sum y_kL_k$ takes the value $y_k$ at $x_k$.

The numerator of $L_k$ has a factor $(x - x_j)$ for every node except $x_k$, so $L_k$ vanishes at those $n$ nodes; the denominator is the same product evaluated at $x_k$, so $L_k(x_k) = 1$. Each $L_k$ has degree $n$, so $p$ has degree at most $n$. Uniqueness: if $p$ and $q$ both interpolate, $p - q$ has degree at most $n$ but vanishes at $n + 1$ different nodes. A nonzero polynomial of degree at most $n$ has at most $n$ roots, so $p - q = 0$.

blocks.q: Find the polynomial of degree at most 3 through $(0, 1)$, $(1, 3)$, $(2, 5)$, $(3, 7)$.
steps: The four points lie on the line $y = 2x + 1$.
That line is a polynomial of degree at most 3 through all four points, and the interpolant is unique, so it is the interpolant.
Four points do not force degree 3; they allow it. The Lagrange formula would give the same line after the $x^{3}$ and $x^{2}$ terms cancel.

blocks.html: The Lagrange form is perfect for proving things and for seeing the structure: the interpolant depends linearly on the data $y_k$. For computing with many points or adding points one at a time, Newton's divided differences are handier, and for large $n$ a rearrangement called the barycentric formula is both fast and numerically stable. All of them produce the same polynomial.

Expecting degree $n + 1$ for $n + 1$ points (two points determine a line, degree 1), or building a basis polynomial that is $0$ at the wrong nodes, for example including the factor $(x - x_k)$ in $L_k$. Check each $L_k$ by plugging in the nodes: it must give $1$ at $x_k$ and $0$ at all the others.

blocks.html: The Lagrange form has a drawback: add one more data point and every basis polynomial changes. Newton's form builds the same interpolating polynomial one point at a time: $$p(x) = c_0 + c_1(x - x_0) + c_2(x - x_0)(x - x_1) + \cdots + c_n(x - x_0)\cdots(x - x_{n-1}).$$ Each new term vanishes at all the earlier nodes, so it never spoils the fit already made.

The coefficients are divided differences, defined recursively: $f[x_i] = y_i$ and $$f[x_i, \ldots, x_j] = \frac{f[x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_j] - f[x_i, \ldots, x_{j-1}]}{x_j - x_i}.$$ Then $c_k = f[x_0, \ldots, x_k]$, the top edge of the divided-difference table.

Fill the table column by column: each entry is (lower-left entry − upper-left entry) divided by the difference of the $x$-values at the two ends of its span. The top entries are the Newton coefficients, and adding a point adds one row and one coefficient.

$c_0 = y_0$ makes $p(x_0)$ right; $c_1 = \frac{y_1 - y_0}{x_1 - x_0}$ (a slope) makes $p(x_1)$ right. In general $c_k$ is the leading coefficient of the polynomial through $x_0, \ldots, x_k$. If $p_{\mathrm{L}}$ interpolates at $x_0, \ldots, x_{k-1}$ and $p_{\mathrm{R}}$ at $x_1, \ldots, x_k$, then $$\frac{(x - x_0)p_{\mathrm{R}}(x) - (x - x_k)p_{\mathrm{L}}(x)}{x_k - x_0}$$ has degree at most $k$ and matches all $k + 1$ points (check the middle nodes, then $x_0$ and $x_k$). Comparing leading coefficients gives exactly the recursion, with $x_k - x_0$, the ends of the span, in the denominator.

blocks.title: A table for three points
blocks.q: Find the Newton form of the polynomial through $(0, 1)$, $(1, 3)$, $(3, 2)$.
steps: Second difference: $f[0, 1, 3] = \frac{-\frac{1}{2} - 2}{3 - 0} = -\frac{5}{6}$. The denominator is $3 - 0$, the ends of the span.
$p(x) = 1 + 2x - \frac{5}{6}x(x - 1)$, which expands to $-\frac{5}{6}x^{2} + \frac{17}{6}x + 1$: the same polynomial the Lagrange form gave.

blocks.title: Adding a point
blocks.q: Add the point $(4, 5)$ to the data above.
steps: New entries along the bottom: $f[3, 4] = \frac{5 - 2}{4 - 3} = 3$, then $f[1, 3, 4] = \frac{3 - (-\frac{1}{2})}{4 - 1} = \frac{7}{6}$.
New polynomial: the old one plus $\frac{1}{2}x(x - 1)(x - 3)$. At the old nodes the new term is $0$; at $x = 4$: old value $1$, plus $\frac{1}{2}(4)(3)(1) = 6$, total $5$. ✓

blocks.html: Newton's form is also cheap to evaluate. Nest it like Horner's method: $p(x) = c_0 + (x - x_0)\big(c_1 + (x - x_1)(c_2 + \cdots)\big)$, one multiplication and two additions per coefficient. Building the table takes about $n^{2}/2$ divisions, far less than solving the $(n + 1) \times (n + 1)$ system for the ordinary coefficients.

Dividing by the gap between neighboring $x$-values at every level. Only the first column uses neighbors; the entry $f[x_i, \ldots, x_j]$ always divides by $x_j - x_i$, the outermost pair. With equally spaced nodes the mistake changes every entry by a constant factor, so it is easy to miss; with uneven spacing it gives a polynomial that misses the data. Check: the finished polynomial must reproduce every data point.

blocks.html: An interpolating polynomial matches the data at the nodes. How far is it from the function in between? The answer looks just like the Taylor remainder, with one important new piece, and it uses the polynomial from Newton's Divided Differences or any other form, since they are all the same polynomial.

If $f$ has $n + 1$ continuous derivatives and $p$ (degree at most $n$) interpolates $f$ at $x_0, \ldots, x_n$, then for each $x$ there is a $\xi$ in the smallest interval containing $x$ and the nodes with $$f(x) - p(x) = \frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n + 1)!}\,\omega(x),\qquad \omega(x) = (x - x_0)(x - x_1)\cdots(x - x_n).$$

Fix an $x$ that is not a node and let $g(t) = f(t) - p(t) - \big(f(x) - p(x)\big)\frac{\omega(t)}{\omega(x)}$. Then $g$ is $0$ at the $n + 1$ nodes and at $t = x$: $n + 2$ zeros. By Rolle's theorem $g'$ has $n + 1$ zeros, $g''$ has $n$, and so on, until $g^{(n+1)}$ has at least one zero $\xi$. But $p^{(n+1)} = 0$ and $\omega^{(n+1)} = (n + 1)!$, so $0 = f^{(n+1)}(\xi) - \big(f(x) - p(x)\big)\frac{(n + 1)!}{\omega(x)}$. Solve for $f(x) - p(x)$.

Two factors control the error. The derivative factor depends on $f$; you cannot change it. The node product $\omega(x)$ depends only on where the nodes are: it is small among the nodes and grows quickly outside them, and for equally spaced nodes it is much larger near the ends of the interval than in the middle.

blocks.title: An exact error
blocks.q: Let $p$ interpolate $f(x) = x^{3}$ at $0, 1, 2$. Find $f(3) - p(3)$ and then $p(3)$, without finding $p$.
steps: Here $f'''(x) = 6$ is constant, so the formula is exact: $f(x) - p(x) = \frac{6}{3!}x(x - 1)(x - 2) = x(x - 1)(x - 2)$.

blocks.title: A bound

blocks.html: It seems obvious that more data points give a better fit. For polynomial interpolation at equally spaced points it is false, and the classic example is Runge's function $f(x) = \frac{1}{1 + 25x^{2}}$ on $[-1, 1]$. The error formula explains why, and a choice of nodes based on the unit circle fixes it.

blocks.html: Two things go wrong at the same time. The derivatives $f^{(n+1)}$ of Runge's function grow very fast with $n$ (it has poles at $x = \pm\frac{i}{5}$ in the complex plane, close to the interval). And for equally spaced nodes the node product $\omega(x)$ is far larger in the outer gaps than in the middle. Together they win over the $(n + 1)!$ in the denominator.

The cure is to choose nodes that keep $|\omega(x)|$ small everywhere. The Chebyshev nodes on $[-1, 1]$ are $$x_k = \cos\frac{(2k + 1)\pi}{2(n + 1)},\quad k = 0, 1, \ldots, n:$$ the $x$-coordinates of points equally spaced in angle around the upper half of the unit circle. They crowd toward the ends of the interval.

With Chebyshev nodes, $\omega(x) = \frac{T_{n+1}(x)}{2^{n}}$, so $\max|\omega| = 2^{-n}$: the smallest possible for $n + 1$ nodes, with all its ripples the same height. For smooth functions like Runge's, the Chebyshev interpolants converge as $n$ grows.

The Chebyshev polynomial $T_m$ is defined by $T_m(\cos\theta) = \cos(m\theta)$; it is a polynomial in $x = \cos\theta$ of degree $m$ with leading coefficient $2^{m-1}$. Its zeros are where $m\theta$ is an odd multiple of $\frac{\pi}{2}$, which are exactly the Chebyshev nodes for $m = n + 1$. So $\omega$, the monic polynomial with those zeros, equals $T_{n+1}/2^{n}$, and since $|\cos| \le 1$, $|\omega(x)| \le 2^{-n}$, with equality at $n + 2$ points. One can show no other monic polynomial of degree $n + 1$ stays smaller on all of $[-1, 1]$.

blocks.html: One polynomial through many points can wiggle badly (see Runge's Phenomenon and Chebyshev Nodes). A spline uses a separate low-degree polynomial on each interval between data points, like interpolation done locally, and joins the pieces smoothly. Cubic pieces are the standard choice.

Given knots $x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_n$ and values $y_i$, a cubic spline $s$ is a cubic polynomial on each $[x_i, x_{i+1}]$, passes through every $(x_i, y_i)$, and has $s$, $s'$ and $s''$ continuous at every inside knot. A natural spline also has $s''(x_0) = s''(x_n) = 0$.

$n$ cubic pieces have $4n$ coefficients. Interpolation gives $2n$ conditions and smoothness of $s'$ and $s''$ at the $n - 1$ inside knots gives $2(n - 1)$ more, leaving $2$: the end conditions. Writing $M_i = s''(x_i)$, equal spacing $h$ leads to the tridiagonal system $$M_{i-1} + 4M_i + M_{i+1} = \frac{6}{h^{2}}(y_{i-1} - 2y_i + y_{i+1}).$$

On each interval $s$ is cubic, so $s''$ is linear: it is the straight line from $M_i$ to $M_{i+1}$, which makes $s''$ continuous automatically. Integrating twice and choosing the two constants so that $s(x_i) = y_i$ and $s(x_{i+1}) = y_{i+1}$ gives, with $h = x_{i+1} - x_i$, $$s(x) = M_i\frac{(x_{i+1} - x)^{3}}{6h} + M_{i+1}\frac{(x - x_i)^{3}}{6h} + \left(\frac{y_i}{h} - \frac{M_ih}{6}\right)(x_{i+1} - x) + \left(\frac{y_{i+1}}{h} - \frac{M_{i+1}h}{6}\right)(x - x_i).$$ Requiring $s'$ to match at each inside knot gives one equation per knot, the system above. It is diagonally dominant ($4 > 1 + 1$), so it can be solved by LU without pivoting in about $8n$ operations.

blocks.html: A derivative is a limit of difference quotients. A computer cannot take the limit, so it stops at a small $h$, and the Truncation Error and Order of Accuracy that leaves depends on which difference quotient we use. Taylor series tell us exactly how big it is.

items: Forward: $f'(x) \approx \dfrac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$.
Backward: $f'(x) \approx \dfrac{f(x) - f(x - h)}{h}$.
Central: $f'(x) \approx \dfrac{f(x + h) - f(x - h)}{2h}$.
Second derivative: $f''(x) \approx \dfrac{f(x + h) - 2f(x) + f(x - h)}{h^{2}}$.

blocks.html: The forward (and backward) difference has error $\frac{h}{2}f''(x) + O(h^{2})$: order $h$. The central difference has error $\frac{h^{2}}{6}f'''(x) + O(h^{4})$: order $h^{2}$. The second-difference formula has error $\frac{h^{2}}{12}f^{(4)}(x) + O(h^{4})$. For the same $h$ and about the same work, the central difference is usually far more accurate.

Write the Taylor expansions $$f(x \pm h) = f(x) \pm hf'(x) + \frac{h^{2}}{2}f''(x) \pm \frac{h^{3}}{6}f'''(x) + \frac{h^{4}}{24}f^{(4)}(x) \pm \cdots$$ The forward quotient keeps the $\frac{h}{2}f''$ term. Subtracting the two expansions cancels every even power, so the central quotient's error starts at $\frac{h^{2}}{6}f'''$. Adding them cancels every odd power, which gives the second-difference formula with error $\frac{h^{2}}{12}f^{(4)}$. The symmetry of the central formulas is what buys the extra order.

blocks.html: Dividing the central difference by $h$ instead of $2h$. The two sample points $x - h$ and $x + h$ are $2h$ apart, so the slope between them divides by $2h$. Dividing by $h$ doubles the answer, a mistake no small $h$ will fix. Quick check: a forward difference with the same $h$ should come out close to your central value, not near half of it.

blocks.html: Finite-Difference Derivatives get better as $h$ shrinks, so why not take $h = 10^{-15}$? Because $f(x + h)$ and $f(x)$ become nearly equal, and subtracting them is Round-Off and Cancellation. Each stored value of $f$ has a rounding error of size about $\varepsilon|f|$ (with $\varepsilon \approx 10^{-16}$), and dividing their difference by a tiny $h$ magnifies that error.

For the forward difference (with $|f| \approx 1$ and $|f''| \le M$) the two errors add up to about $$E(h) = \underbrace{\frac{M}{2}h}_{\text{truncation}} + \underbrace{\frac{2\varepsilon}{h}}_{\text{round-off}}.$$ The first term falls as $h$ shrinks; the second grows.

The total error is smallest at a moderate $h$. For the forward difference, $h^{*} = 2\sqrt{\varepsilon/M} \approx 10^{-8}$ and the best error is about $10^{-8}$: only half the digits survive. For the central difference, $h^{*} \approx (3\varepsilon/M)^{1/3} \approx 10^{-5}$ and the best error is about $\varepsilon^{2/3} \approx 10^{-11}$.

Minimize $E(h) = \frac{M}{2}h + \frac{2\varepsilon}{h}$: $E'(h) = \frac{M}{2} - \frac{2\varepsilon}{h^{2}} = 0$ gives $h^{*} = 2\sqrt{\varepsilon/M}$, and then $E(h^{*}) = 2\sqrt{M\varepsilon}$, where the two parts are equal. For the central difference, $E(h) = \frac{M}{6}h^{2} + \frac{\varepsilon}{h}$ (now $M$ bounds $|f'''|$), and $E'(h) = \frac{M}{3}h - \frac{\varepsilon}{h^{2}} = 0$ gives $h^{*} = (3\varepsilon/M)^{1/3}$. A higher-order formula lets you stop at a larger $h$, before round-off has grown much.

blocks.html: If we know the form of a method's error, we can cancel its leading term by combining two results. For a central difference, $$D(h) = f'(x) + c_2h^{2} + c_4h^{4} + \cdots$$ The constants $c_2, c_4$ are unknown, but they are the same for every $h$, and that is enough.

If $A(h) = A + ch^{p} + O(h^{q})$ with $q > p$, then $$A \approx \frac{2^{p}A(h/2) - A(h)}{2^{p} - 1},$$ with error $O(h^{q})$. For an $h^{2}$ error: $\frac{4A(h/2) - A(h)}{3}$. For an $h$ error: $2A(h/2) - A(h)$. As a bonus, $\frac{A(h/2) - A(h)}{2^{p} - 1}$ estimates the error of $A(h/2)$.

Write the two results: $A(h) = A + ch^{p} + \cdots$ and $A(h/2) = A + \frac{c}{2^{p}}h^{p} + \cdots$. Multiply the second by $2^{p}$ and subtract the first: the $ch^{p}$ terms cancel, leaving $(2^{p} - 1)A$ plus higher-order terms. Divide by $2^{p} - 1$. For the error estimate, subtract instead: $A(h/2) - A(h) \approx -\frac{2^{p} - 1}{2^{p}}ch^{p} = (2^{p} - 1)\big(A(h/2) - A\big)$.

blocks.html: Extrapolation is cheap: it needs no new function values, only arithmetic on results already computed. It is also a safety check. If the extrapolated value and $A(h/2)$ differ by much more than the estimated error, the assumed form of the error is wrong, perhaps because $h$ is not yet small enough.

The idea goes further: with three results one can cancel two error terms, and repeating it on the trapezoid rule gives Romberg integration. The one requirement is that the error really behaves like $ch^{p}$; for a function that is not smooth enough, or with $h$ so small that round-off matters, extrapolation does not help.

Using the weights for the wrong order. $\frac{4A(h/2) - A(h)}{3}$ cancels an $h^{2}$ term; $2A(h/2) - A(h)$ cancels an $h$ term; $\frac{16A(h/2) - A(h)}{15}$ cancels $h^{4}$. Check the order of your method first (or measure it from three results), then use $2^{p}$.

blocks.html: You have used the trapezoid and Simpson's rules with their error bounds in Trapezoid and Simpson's Rules. Here we read those bounds as statements about order: how fast does the error shrink as the panels get thinner, and for which functions is a rule exact?

With step $h = \frac{b - a}{n}$, the composite trapezoid rule has error $-\frac{(b - a)h^{2}}{12}f''(\xi)$: order $h^{2}$. Composite Simpson's rule has error $-\frac{(b - a)h^{4}}{180}f^{(4)}(\xi)$: order $h^{4}$. Doubling $n$ cuts the errors by about 4 and 16. Simpson's rule is exact for every cubic.

On one panel the trapezoid rule integrates the line through the endpoints; by the interpolation error formula the gap is $\frac{f''(\xi)}{2}(x - x_i)(x - x_{i+1})$, whose integral over the panel is $-\frac{h^{3}}{12}f''$. There are $n = \frac{b - a}{h}$ panels, so the total is $-\frac{(b - a)h^{2}}{12}f''$ for some average point: one power of $h$ is lost in the sum. Simpson's rule integrates a parabola through three points, which should make it exact only for quadratics. But it is symmetric about the middle point, so it also integrates the odd function $(x - m)^{3}$ exactly (both sides give 0). Hence it is exact for cubics, and its error involves $f^{(4)}$.

blocks.html: The trapezoid rule's error is not just $O(h^{2})$: for a smooth integrand it is a whole series in even powers, $$T(h) = I + c_1h^{2} + c_2h^{4} + c_3h^{6} + \cdots$$ (the Euler–Maclaurin formula). Richardson extrapolation can cancel these terms one after another, using trapezoid values with $h$ halved each time.

Fill a triangle: $R(k, 0) = T(h/2^{k})$, and $$R(k, m) = \frac{4^{m}R(k, m - 1) - R(k - 1, m - 1)}{4^{m} - 1}.$$ Column $m$ has error $O(h^{2m + 2})$. Column 1 is Simpson's rule; column 2 is Boole's rule.

Each column removes the next even power. Column 0 has error $c_1h^{2} + \cdots$; halving $h$ divides the $h^{2}$ term by 4, so $\frac{4R(k, 0) - R(k - 1, 0)}{3}$ removes it and leaves $O(h^{4})$. In column 1 the leading term is $h^{4}$, which halving divides by $16 = 4^{2}$, so the factor becomes 16. In column $m$ it is $4^{m}$. And halving $h$ in the trapezoid rule reuses all the old points: only the new midpoints need new function values.

blocks.html: In practice the triangle grows one row at a time, and the computation stops when two neighboring diagonal entries agree to the required tolerance. For smooth integrands this converges very fast. It relies on the even-power error series, so it works poorly for integrands with a singularity or a kink; adaptive integration handles those better.

Cost: row $k$ needs the trapezoid rule with $2^{k}$ panels, but only its $2^{k-1}$ new midpoints are new function values. The whole triangle up to row $k$ therefore costs $2^{k} + 1$ evaluations of $f$, the same as the single finest trapezoid rule; the extrapolation itself is nearly free.

Using the factor 4 in every column. Only column 1 uses 4; column 2 needs 16 and column $m$ needs $4^{m}$. Using 4 again cancels the $h^{2}$ term that is already gone and leaves the $h^{4}$ term in place, so the column gives no improvement. Check: each column should agree with the true value to clearly more digits than the column before.

blocks.html: The trapezoid and Simpson rules use equally spaced points and choose only the weights. Gauss had a better idea: choose the points too. With $n$ points there are $2n$ numbers to choose, so a rule can be made exact for all polynomials of degree up to $2n - 1$, which is what interpolation at $n$ fixed points could never do.

Two-point Gauss rule: $\int_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,dx \approx f\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) + f\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)$, exact for every cubic. In general the $n$-point Gauss–Legendre rule is exact up to degree $2n - 1$ (three points: nodes $0, \pm\sqrt{3/5}$, weights $\frac{8}{9}, \frac{5}{9}, \frac{5}{9}$). On $[a, b]$, substitute $x = \frac{a + b}{2} + \frac{b - a}{2}t$ and multiply by $\frac{b - a}{2}$.

Ask for $w_1f(x_1) + w_2f(x_2)$ to equal $\int_{-1}^{1}f$ for $f = 1, x, x^{2}, x^{3}$: $$w_1 + w_2 = 2,\quad w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 = 0,\quad w_1x_1^{2} + w_2x_2^{2} = \tfrac{2}{3},\quad w_1x_1^{3} + w_2x_2^{3} = 0.$$ By symmetry try $x_2 = -x_1$, $w_1 = w_2 = 1$: the odd equations hold automatically, and $2x_1^{2} = \frac{2}{3}$ gives $x_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$. For the interval $[a, b]$, the substitution maps $[-1, 1]$ onto $[a, b]$ and $dx = \frac{b - a}{2}\,dt$, which is where the extra factor comes from.

blocks.html: Where do the nodes come from in general? They are the zeros of the Legendre polynomial $P_n$, the polynomials that are orthogonal on $[-1, 1]$; that orthogonality is exactly what makes the rule exact up to degree $2n - 1$. The weights are all positive, which keeps the rule stable. The price: the nodes for $n$ and $n + 1$ points share nothing (apart from $0$), so increasing $n$ throws away all earlier function values. Practical codes therefore use a fixed $n$ on many panels (composite Gauss), or pairs of rules built to share nodes (Gauss–Kronrod), which also give an error estimate.

blocks.html: Many integrands are easy almost everywhere and hard in a few places: a spike, a corner, a steep start. Spreading panels evenly wastes effort on the easy parts. Adaptive integration puts small panels only where they are needed, and it decides where by using Richardson's idea on Simpson's rule as an error estimate.

items: On $[a, b]$ compute $S_1$, Simpson's rule on the whole interval, and $S_2$, Simpson's rule on each half, added.
Estimate the error of $S_2$ by $\frac{|S_2 - S_1|}{15}$.
If it is at most the tolerance for this interval, accept $S_2 + \frac{S_2 - S_1}{15}$ (or simply $S_2$).
Otherwise split the interval in two, give each half half the tolerance, and repeat on each half.

blocks.html: Simpson's error is about $Ch^{4}$, so halving $h$ divides it by 16 and $S_2 - S_1 \approx 15 \times (\text{error of } S_2)$. Only the intervals that fail the test are split, so the panels end up small exactly where the integrand is hard.

If $S_1 \approx I + Ch^{4}$, then $S_2 \approx I + C\frac{h^{4}}{16}$ (the constant $C$ involves $f^{(4)}$, nearly the same on a small interval). Subtracting, $S_2 - S_1 \approx -\frac{15}{16}Ch^{4} = -15\,(S_2 - I)$, so $I - S_2 \approx \frac{S_2 - S_1}{15}$. The estimate costs only two new function values, since $S_2$ reuses the three points of $S_1$. Halving the tolerance with each split keeps the total error within the original tolerance.

steps: Estimate: $\frac{S_2 - S_1}{15} = \frac{-0.25}{15} \approx -0.016667$. True error of $S_2$: $6.4 - 6.41667 = -0.016667$. Identical, because $f^{(4)}$ is constant.

steps: That exceeds $10^{-5}$: split into two halves, each with tolerance $5 \times 10^{-6}$.

Intervals near $0$ keep failing the test and get split again and again; on $[\frac{1}{2}, 1]$ one or two panels pass at once.
The panels shrink geometrically toward $0$. A uniform grid fine enough for $0$ would waste thousands of function values on the easy part.

blocks.html: In Improved Euler and Runge–Kutta Methods you met Euler's method, $y_{n+1} = y_n + hf(t_n, y_n)$, and the more accurate Heun and Runge–Kutta methods. Now we measure their error the way Truncation Error and Order of Accuracy taught: by how it shrinks with $h$. There are two different errors to keep apart.

The local error is the error of one step taken from an exact value: $y(t_n + h)$ minus the step's result when $y_n = y(t_n)$. The global error is what we actually care about: $y(T) - y_N$ at the final time, after all $N = T/h$ steps.

For a method of order $p$, the local error is $O(h^{p+1})$ and the global error is $O(h^{p})$: summing about $1/h$ local errors costs one power of $h$. Euler: local $O(h^{2})$, global $O(h)$. Heun: global $O(h^{2})$. RK4: global $O(h^{4})$.

For Euler, Taylor's theorem gives $y(t + h) = y(t) + hy'(t) + \frac{h^{2}}{2}y''(\xi)$, and the step keeps only the first two terms: local error $\frac{h^{2}}{2}y''$. Over $[0, T]$ there are $N = T/h$ steps. Each adds an error of size about $Ch^{2}$, and earlier errors are carried along (grown or damped by the equation by at most a factor $e^{LT}$, where $L$ bounds $|\partial f/\partial y|$). So the global error is at most about $N \cdot Ch^{2}\,e^{LT} = CTe^{LT}h$: order $h$.

blocks.html: Every one-step method works on vectors as well as numbers. Any higher-order equation becomes a first-order system, as in Systems in Matrix Form, and then Euler, Heun or RK4 run with each $y$ replaced by a vector $\mathbf{u}$ and each $f$ by a vector function $\mathbf{F}$. The error orders stay the same.

To solve $y'' = f(t, y, y')$, set $u_1 = y$, $u_2 = y'$: $$u_1' = u_2,\qquad u_2' = f(t, u_1, u_2).$$ Each component needs its own starting value, so the problem must give both $y(0)$ and $y'(0)$. Then step all components together, always using values from the same stage.

The derivation of each method (Taylor expansion, or averaging slopes) never used that $y$ was a single number; it works component by component. What must not happen is mixing stages: in Euler's method both components of $\mathbf{u}_{n+1}$ are computed from the old $\mathbf{u}_n$. Updating $u_1$ first and then using the new $u_1$ in $u_2$ is a different method, with different behavior.

Systems also show why stability matters: the components can decay or oscillate at very different rates, set by the eigenvalues of $A$, and a step size must suit all of them. That is the subject of Stability of Euler's Method.

Without $y'(0)$ the first step of $u_1' = u_2$ cannot even begin. Also keep the stages straight: Euler uses the old values for every component.

blocks.html: A method with small truncation error can still produce garbage if the step is too big, even when the true solution is perfectly calm. To see why, apply it to the test equation $$y' = \lambda y,\qquad \text{Re}\,\lambda < 0,$$ whose solution $y_0e^{\lambda t}$ decays. This is the ODE version of algorithm stability.

Euler's method gives $y_{n+1} = y_n + h\lambda y_n = (1 + h\lambda)y_n$, so $$y_n = (1 + h\lambda)^{n}y_0.$$ Every one-step method turns into $y_{n+1} = R(h\lambda)\,y_n$ for some function $R$, its amplification factor.

The computed values stay bounded only when $|R(h\lambda)| \le 1$. For forward Euler, $R(z) = 1 + z$, so $h\lambda$ must lie in the disk of radius 1 centered at $-1$; for real $\lambda < 0$ that means $h \le \frac{2}{|\lambda|}$. For a system $\mathbf{y}' = A\mathbf{y}$, every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $A$ must satisfy the condition.

The exact solution decays because $|e^{h\lambda}| < 1$. The method replaces $e^{h\lambda}$ by $R(h\lambda)$, which is accurate for small $|h\lambda|$ (it matches the Taylor series of $e^{z}$ up to the method's order) but can be larger than 1 in size when $|h\lambda|$ is large. Then $|R|^{n}$ grows without bound, and any error, even round-off, is magnified each step. For a system, diagonalizing $A$ splits it into separate test equations, one per eigenvalue, so the step must suit the eigenvalue farthest from the origin.

blocks.html: The stability limit of explicit methods is a disaster for stiff problems. The fix is to use the slope at the new point: $$y_{n+1} = y_n + hf(t_{n+1}, y_{n+1}).$$ This is backward Euler. The unknown $y_{n+1}$ appears on both sides, so each step means solving an equation: an implicit method.

For $y' = \lambda y$, backward Euler gives $y_{n+1} = \frac{y_n}{1 - h\lambda}$. When $\text{Re}\,\lambda < 0$, $\left|\frac{1}{1 - h\lambda}\right| < 1$ for every $h > 0$: no step-size limit from stability. The price is solving for $y_{n+1}$ each step (a division, a linear system, or Newton's method), and the accuracy is still only first order.

From $y_{n+1} = y_n + h\lambda y_{n+1}$ we get $(1 - h\lambda)y_{n+1} = y_n$. If $\text{Re}\,\lambda < 0$ and $h > 0$, then $\text{Re}(1 - h\lambda) > 1$, so $|1 - h\lambda| > 1$ and the factor is smaller than 1 in size: the computed solution decays, as the true one does. Geometrically, backward Euler's stability region is everything outside the disk of radius 1 centered at $+1$, which contains the whole left half-plane. A method stable on the whole left half-plane is called A-stable.

blocks.html: A problem is stiff when it has components that decay much faster than the solution you want to follow. Explicit methods must use steps small enough for the fastest component; implicit methods may use steps chosen for accuracy alone. That trade (more work per step, far fewer steps) is why stiff solvers are implicit.

Taking the backward Euler step with the slope at the old point. $y_{n+1} = y_n + hf(t_n, y_n)$ is forward Euler again, with all its stability limits, whatever it is called. Check: the unknown $y_{n+1}$ must appear inside $f$, and you must solve for it.

blocks.html: Runge–Kutta methods spend several evaluations of $f$ per step and then forget them. Multistep methods keep the slopes from earlier steps and reuse them, so each step needs only one new evaluation of $f$. Their accuracy is measured just as in Local and Global Error.
The two-step Adams–Bashforth method (AB2) is $$y_{n+1} = y_n + \frac{h}{2}\big(3f_n - f_{n-1}\big),\qquad f_k = f(t_k, y_k).$$

Adams–Bashforth methods integrate a polynomial through earlier slopes. The $k$-step method has order $k$ and uses one new $f$ value per step, but it needs $k - 1$ extra starting values, which a one-step method (such as RK4) must supply.

Exactly, $y(t_{n+1}) = y(t_n) + \int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}f(t, y(t))\,dt$. Replace $f$ by the line through $(t_{n-1}, f_{n-1})$ and $(t_n, f_n)$ and integrate it over $[t_n, t_{n+1}]$: the line has value $f_n$ at $t_n$ and $f_n + (f_n - f_{n-1})$ at $t_{n+1}$, so its average over the step is $\frac{3f_n - f_{n-1}}{2}$. The interpolation error is $O(h^{2})$, which gives local error $O(h^{3})$ and global error $O(h^{2})$. Using more past slopes gives higher order in the same way.

blocks.html: A boundary value problem fixes $y$ at both ends of an interval instead of giving $y$ and $y'$ at the start, so stepping forward from one end does not work directly. Instead, put a grid on the interval, replace $y''$ by the second difference, and solve for all the unknown grid values at once with a linear system, using Solving with PA = LU.

For $y'' = f(x)$ on $[a, b]$ with $y(a) = \alpha$, $y(b) = \beta$, take $x_i = a + ih$, $i = 0, \ldots, N$, with $h = \frac{b - a}{N}$. The unknowns are $y_1, \ldots, y_{N-1}$; $y_0 = \alpha$ and $y_N = \beta$ are known. At each inside point, $$y_{i-1} - 2y_i + y_{i+1} = h^{2}f(x_i).$$

The equations form a tridiagonal system: $1, -2, 1$ around the diagonal. In the first and last equations the known boundary values move to the right-hand side. The error at the grid points is $O(h^{2})$, and the system is solved in $O(N)$ operations.

The second difference has truncation error $\frac{h^{2}}{12}y^{(4)}$, so the discrete equations differ from the true ones by $O(h^{2})$; for this kind of problem that carries over to the computed values. Each equation involves only three neighbors, so the matrix is tridiagonal. It is also symmetric and diagonally dominant (weakly), so elimination needs no pivoting and costs about $8N$ operations instead of $\frac{2}{3}N^{3}$.

blocks.html: The The Heat Equation, $u_t = ku_{xx}$, describes heat spreading along a rod. To compute it, combine two ideas you already have: the second difference in space from Boundary Value Problems by Finite Differences, and a forward Euler step in time, whose stability limits will matter.

On a grid $x_i = i\Delta x$, $t_n = n\Delta t$, write $u_i^{n} \approx u(x_i, t_n)$. The explicit scheme is $$u_i^{n+1} = u_i^{n} + r\left(u_{i+1}^{n} - 2u_i^{n} + u_{i-1}^{n}\right),\qquad r = \frac{k\Delta t}{\Delta x^{2}},$$ with the end values given by the boundary conditions.
The explicit scheme is stable only when $r \le \frac{1}{2}$, that is, $\Delta t \le \frac{\Delta x^{2}}{2k}$. Refining the space grid by a factor of 2 forces 4 times as many time steps.

Two views. First, rewrite the update as $u_i^{n+1} = ru_{i-1}^{n} + (1 - 2r)u_i^{n} + ru_{i+1}^{n}$. When $r \le \frac{1}{2}$ all three weights are nonnegative and add to 1, so each new value is an average of old ones and nothing can grow. Second, try the sawtooth $u_i = (-1)^{i}$: then $u_{i+1} - 2u_i + u_{i-1} = -4u_i$, so the sawtooth is multiplied by $1 - 4r$ each step. $|1 - 4r| \le 1$ exactly when $r \le \frac{1}{2}$; otherwise it grows and flips sign every step. (In method-of-lines terms, the fastest mode is $y' = \lambda y$ with $\lambda \approx -\frac{4k}{\Delta x^{2}}$, and Euler needs $\Delta t|\lambda| \le 2$.)

blocks.title: The cost of refining
blocks.q: For $k = 1$ and $\Delta x = 0.1$, find the largest stable $\Delta t$. What happens if $\Delta x$ is halved?
steps: Twice the grid points and 4 times the steps: 8 times the work to reach the same final time. In two space dimensions the same refinement costs 16 times as much.

blocks.title: How fast instability wins
blocks.q: With $r = 0.6$, a sawtooth of size $10^{-16}$ (round-off) is present. How big is it after 100 steps?
steps: $1.4^{100} \approx 4 \times 10^{14}$, so it reaches about $4 \times 10^{14} \times 10^{-16} = 0.04$, and a few dozen steps later it dominates the solution.

blocks.html: Refining the space grid without shrinking the time step. Halving $\Delta x$ quadruples $r$, which can push a stable computation past $r = \frac{1}{2}$. Always recompute $r = \frac{k\Delta t}{\Delta x^{2}}$ after changing either step. (Implicit schemes, such as backward Euler or Crank–Nicolson in time, remove this limit.)

blocks.html: In Least Squares you found the $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ that makes $\lVert\mathbf{b} - A\mathbf{x}\rVert_2$ as small as possible by solving the normal equations $A^{T}A\hat{\mathbf{x}} = A^{T}\mathbf{b}$. In exact arithmetic that is fine. In floating point it can throw away half of the available digits, for a reason you met in The Condition Number of a Matrix.

Factor the $m \times n$ matrix $A$ (with $m > n$ and independent columns) as $A = QR$, as in Gram–Schmidt and QR: $Q$ is $m \times n$ with orthonormal columns ($Q^{T}Q = I$) and $R$ is $n \times n$, upper triangular and invertible.

The least-squares solution solves the triangular system $$R\hat{\mathbf{x}} = Q^{T}\mathbf{b},$$ by back substitution. This avoids $A^{T}A$, whose condition number is $\kappa_2(A^{T}A) = \kappa_2(A)^{2}$. With QR the loss of digits is governed by $\kappa_2(A)$ (for problems that fit the data well); with the normal equations it is governed by $\kappa_2(A)^{2}$.

Substitute $A = QR$ into the normal equations: $A^{T}A = R^{T}Q^{T}QR = R^{T}R$ and $A^{T}\mathbf{b} = R^{T}Q^{T}\mathbf{b}$, so $R^{T}R\hat{\mathbf{x}} = R^{T}Q^{T}\mathbf{b}$. Since $R^{T}$ is invertible, cancel it: $R\hat{\mathbf{x}} = Q^{T}\mathbf{b}$. For the conditioning, the singular values of $A^{T}A$ are the squares $\sigma_i^{2}$ of those of $A$, so $\kappa_2(A^{T}A) = \frac{\sigma_1^{2}}{\sigma_n^{2}} = \kappa_2(A)^{2}$. Multiplying by $Q^{T}$ never changes lengths of vectors in the column space, so it adds no amplification of its own.

blocks.title: Where the normal equations break
blocks.q: Let $\delta = 10^{-8}$, $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ \delta & 0 \\ 0 & \delta \end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{b} = (2, \delta, \delta)$, so the exact solution is $(1, 1)$. Compare the two methods in double precision.
steps: $A^{T}A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 + \delta^{2} & 1 \\ 1 & 1 + \delta^{2} \end{bmatrix}$, and $1 + 10^{-16}$ rounds to $1$ (it is less than half a gap above $1$).
So the computed $A^{T}A$ is $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, which is singular: the normal equations have no unique solution at all.
QR computed with Householder reflections (the way libraries do it) returns $(1, 1)$ to full accuracy here, even though $\kappa_2(A) \approx 1.4 \times 10^{8}$.

blocks.title: Counting digits
blocks.q: A least-squares problem has $\kappa_2(A) = 10^{5}$. About how many correct digits can each method give in double precision (about 16 digits)?
steps: QR: lose up to about $5$ digits, leaving about $11$.
Normal equations: $\kappa_2(A^{T}A) = 10^{10}$, so lose up to about $10$, leaving about $6$.

blocks.cap: Fitting polynomials to 30 points in double precision. As the degree grows, κ(A) grows fast. The QR error (green) tracks κ(A)·ε; the normal-equations error (orange) tracks κ(A)²·ε.

blocks.html: The normal equations are not always wrong: they cost about half as much as QR, and when $A$ is well conditioned (say $\kappa_2(A) < 10^{3}$) the lost digits do not matter. But a library cannot know in advance, so it uses QR (or the SVD for the hardest cases). One more caution: classical Gram–Schmidt, done naively in floating point, can lose orthogonality in $Q$; Householder reflections do not.

Forming $A^{T}A$ for every least-squares problem. Since $\kappa(A^{T}A) = \kappa(A)^{2}$, a problem that QR solves to 8 digits can come out with none from the normal equations. Check: estimate $\kappa(A)$; if its square is anywhere near $10^{16}$, do not form $A^{T}A$.
