blocks.html: Finding eigenvalues from the characteristic polynomial is hopeless for large matrices: the roots of a high-degree polynomial are badly conditioned. The simplest practical method only multiplies by $A$. Start from a vector $\mathbf{x}_0$ and repeat: $$\mathbf{y} = A\mathbf{x}_k,\qquad \mu_{k+1} = \text{the entry of }\mathbf{y}\text{ largest in size},\qquad \mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \frac{\mathbf{y}}{\mu_{k+1}}.$$ Scaling keeps the numbers from overflowing; it makes $\lVert\mathbf{x}_{k+1}\rVert_\infty = 1$ (see Vector and Matrix Norms).

If $A$ has a dominant eigenvalue, $|\lambda_1| > |\lambda_2| \ge \cdots$, and $\mathbf{x}_0$ has some component along its eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1$, then $\mathbf{x}_k$ turns toward $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mu_k \to \lambda_1$. The error shrinks by about $\left|\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\right|$ each step.

Write $\mathbf{x}_0 = c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2\mathbf{v}_2 + \cdots + c_n\mathbf{v}_n$ (for a diagonalizable $A$). Then $$A^{k}\mathbf{x}_0 = \lambda_1^{k}\left(c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2\left(\tfrac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\right)^{k}\mathbf{v}_2 + \cdots + c_n\left(\tfrac{\lambda_n}{\lambda_1}\right)^{k}\mathbf{v}_n\right).$$ Every ratio has size less than 1, so every term but the first dies out, the slowest one like $\left|\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\right|^{k}$. Scaling only changes the length, not the direction, so $\mathbf{x}_k$ lines up with $\mathbf{v}_1$, and then $A\mathbf{x}_k \approx \lambda_1\mathbf{x}_k$ makes the scale factor approach $\lambda_1$.

blocks.title: Three steps by hand
blocks.q: Run the power method on $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ from $\mathbf{x}_0 = (1, 0)$. (Its eigenvalues are $3$ and $1$.)
steps: Heading to $\lambda_1 = 3$ and $\mathbf{v}_1 = (1, 1)$; the error in $\mu$ goes $1, 0.5, 0.2$, then $0.071, 0.024$: shrinking by about $\frac{1}{3}$ each step.

blocks.title: How many steps?
blocks.q: About how many steps reduce the error by a factor of $10^{6}$ when $\left|\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\right| = 0.9$? When it is $\frac{1}{3}$?
steps: When the top two eigenvalues are close in size, the power method crawls.

blocks.title: Two eigenvalues of the same size
blocks.q: Run the power method on $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ (eigenvalues $2$ and $-2$) from $\mathbf{x}_0 = (1, 0.5)$.
steps: The iterates bounce between two vectors forever. With $\lambda_2 = -\lambda_1$ the ratio has size exactly $1$, and the $\mathbf{v}_2$ part never fades; it just flips sign each step.

blocks.html: For a symmetric matrix, a better estimate of $\lambda_1$ from the same vector is the Rayleigh quotient $\frac{\mathbf{x}^{T}A\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{x}^{T}\mathbf{x}}$: its error shrinks like $\left|\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\right|^{2k}$, twice as many digits. For $\mathbf{x}_2 = (1, 0.8)$ above it gives $2.976$, already closer than $\mu_4 \approx 2.929$. Search engines once ranked web pages with a power method on a matrix of links.

Expecting convergence when the two largest eigenvalues have the same size, such as $2$ and $-2$, or a complex pair $a \pm bi$. Then no term dominates and the iterates never settle. Check: if the scale factors or vectors keep repeating a pattern instead of settling, look for a tie in size. (The method also fails if $\mathbf{x}_0$ has no $\mathbf{v}_1$ part, though round-off usually adds one.)

blocks.html: The The Power Method finds only the eigenvalue largest in size. To reach any other, apply it to a different matrix with the same eigenvectors. If $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ and $s$ is a number (the shift), then $$(A - sI)^{-1}\mathbf{v} = \frac{1}{\lambda - s}\,\mathbf{v}.$$

Shifted inverse iteration runs the power method on $(A - sI)^{-1}$. It converges to the eigenvector whose eigenvalue $\lambda$ is closest to $s$, and the scale factors settle at $\mu = \frac{1}{\lambda - s}$, so $$\lambda = s + \frac{1}{\mu}.$$ Each step solves $(A - sI)\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}_k$ using one LU factorization made at the start; it never forms the inverse.

The eigenvalues of $(A - sI)^{-1}$ are the numbers $\frac{1}{\lambda_i - s}$. The largest in size comes from the $\lambda_i$ with the smallest $|\lambda_i - s|$, so that is the one the power method finds. Its convergence ratio is the ratio of the two largest sizes, $\frac{|\lambda_{\text{near}} - s|}{|\lambda_{\text{next}} - s|}$, which is tiny when $s$ is a good guess. Factoring $A - sI$ costs about $\frac{2}{3}n^{3}$ once; each step then costs only two triangular solves, about $2n^{2}$.

blocks.title: The smallest eigenvalue
blocks.q: Use inverse iteration with $s = 0$ on $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ from $\mathbf{x}_0 = (1, 0)$.
steps: $\mu$ heads to $1$, so $\lambda = 0 + \frac{1}{1} = 1$, the smallest eigenvalue, with eigenvector $(1, -1)$.

blocks.title: Recovering λ
blocks.q: A matrix has eigenvalues near $1$, $4$ and $10$. With $s = 3.8$, the scale factors settle at $\mu = 5$. Which eigenvalue was found, and how fast was the convergence?
steps: Distances from $s$: $0.2$ to the eigenvalue $4$, $2.8$ to $1$, $6.2$ to $10$.
Ratio $\frac{0.2}{2.8} = \frac{1}{14}$: more than one new digit every step.

blocks.title: A shift too close?
blocks.q: If $s$ is extremely close to an eigenvalue, $A - sI$ is nearly singular. Does that spoil the method?
steps: The computed $\mathbf{y}$ has a large error, but the error is almost entirely along the wanted eigenvector, the direction $(A - sI)^{-1}$ stretches most.
Scaling removes the size, so the direction is still right. A nearly singular $A - sI$ is the method working well, not failing.

blocks.html: Updating the shift every step to the current Rayleigh quotient gives Rayleigh quotient iteration, which for symmetric matrices triples the number of correct digits each step, at the price of a new factorization each time.

Reporting the eigenvalue $\mu$ of $(A - sI)^{-1}$ as the answer. The eigenvalue of $A$ is $s + \frac{1}{\mu}$. Check: your answer should be close to the shift (inverse iteration finds the eigenvalue nearest $s$), and $A\mathbf{x} \approx \lambda\mathbf{x}$ should hold for the final vector.

blocks.html: Before computing eigenvalues, it helps to know roughly where they are: to choose a shift, to check an answer, or to prove a matrix is invertible. Gershgorin's theorem gives such a picture straight from the entries, with no characteristic polynomial at all.

For each row $i$ of an $n \times n$ matrix $A$, draw the disk in the complex plane with center $a_{ii}$ and radius $$r_i = \sum_{j \ne i}|a_{ij}|,$$ the sum of the sizes of the other entries in that row. Every eigenvalue of $A$ lies in at least one of these disks. Moreover, if $k$ disks form a group that does not touch the others, that group holds exactly $k$ eigenvalues (counted with multiplicity).

Let $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ with $\mathbf{v} 
e \mathbf{0}$, and pick $i$ so that $|v_i|$ is the largest entry of $\mathbf{v}$ in size. Row $i$ of $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ says $\sum_j a_{ij}v_j = \lambda v_i$, so $$(\lambda - a_{ii})v_i = \sum_{j 
e i}a_{ij}v_j.$$ Take sizes and divide by $|v_i|$: $|\lambda - a_{ii}| \le \sum_{j 
e i}|a_{ij}| rac{|v_j|}{|v_i|} \le r_i$, since each ratio is at most $1$. So $\lambda$ is in disk $i$. (The counting statement comes from shrinking the off-diagonal entries to $0$ continuously: the eigenvalues move continuously from the centers and cannot jump between separate groups.)

blocks.title: Three separate disks
blocks.q: Locate the eigenvalues of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 \end{bmatrix}$.
steps: Row 1: center $10$, radius $|1| + |-1| = 2$. Row 2: center $0$, radius $1 + 2 = 3$. Row 3: center $-6$, radius $0 + 1 = 1$.
On the real line these are $[8, 12]$, $[-3, 3]$ and $[-7, -5]$: three separate disks, so each holds exactly one eigenvalue.
Each eigenvalue is real: a complex one would come with its conjugate in the same disk (the disks are symmetric about the real axis), making two. The eigenvalues are about $10.09$, $0.23$ and $-6.33$.

blocks.title: Proving a matrix is invertible
blocks.q: Show that $B = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$ is invertible.
steps: Disks: center $5$, radius $3$; center $-4$, radius $3$; center $6$, radius $3$.
None contains $0$ (each $|a_{ii}|$ is bigger than its radius: the matrix is strictly diagonally dominant). So $0$ is not an eigenvalue, and $B$ is invertible.

blocks.title: A disk with no eigenvalue
blocks.q: Draw the disks for $C = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ and find which ones hold the eigenvalues.
steps: Row 1: center $0$, radius $1$. Row 2: center $2$, radius $4$. The disks overlap.
Both lie in the second disk, and neither is within $1$ of $0$: the first disk holds none. The theorem promises only that the union of the overlapping disks holds two.

blocks.html: Because $A$ and $A^{T}$ have the same eigenvalues, column sums give a second set of disks, and the eigenvalues lie in both unions. For symmetric matrices the eigenvalues are real, so the disks become intervals on the real line.

Including $|a_{ii}|$ in the radius, or expecting each disk to hold exactly one eigenvalue. The radius adds only the off-diagonal entries of the row. And when disks overlap, only the group as a whole has a guaranteed count: one disk of the group can hold none. Check: the "exactly one" conclusion needs a disk that touches no other.

blocks.html: The The Power Method finds one eigenvalue at a time. The QR algorithm, the method behind standard eigenvalue routines, finds all of them at once. It uses the QR factorization over and over: $$A_0 = A,\qquad A_k = Q_kR_k\ \ (\text{factor}),\qquad A_{k+1} = R_kQ_k\ \ (\text{multiply in reverse order}).$$

Each $A_{k+1} = Q_k^{T}A_kQ_k$ is similar to $A$, so it has the same eigenvalues. When the eigenvalues have different sizes, $A_k$ approaches an upper triangular matrix, and its diagonal approaches the eigenvalues, largest in size first. The entry below the diagonal in position $(i + 1, i)$ shrinks by about $\left|\frac{\lambda_{i+1}}{\lambda_i}\right|$ each step.

From $A_k = Q_kR_k$ we get $R_k = Q_k^{T}A_k$, so $A_{k+1} = R_kQ_k = Q_k^{T}A_kQ_k$, and $Q_k^{T} = Q_k^{-1}$: a similarity. Why the triangle appears: the product $Q_0Q_1 \cdots Q_{k-1}$ is what you get from running the power method on a whole set of vectors at once, keeping them orthonormal. Its first column turns toward the dominant eigenvector, exactly as in the power method, which pushes the first column of $A_k$ toward $(\lambda_1, 0, \ldots, 0)$; the later columns follow with the next eigenvalues.

blocks.title: One step
blocks.q: Take one step from $A_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.
steps: The first column $(3, 4)$ has length $5$: $\mathbf{q}_1 = (0.6, 0.8)$, and $\mathbf{q}_2 = (-0.8, 0.6)$.
So $A_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 4.76 & -2.68 \\ 0.32 & 0.24 \end{bmatrix}$. Check: the trace is still $5$. The entry below the diagonal fell from $4$ to $0.32$.

blocks.title: Watching it converge
blocks.q: Continue the same example. How fast does the lower-left entry shrink?
steps: $A_2$ has lower-left entry $0.0281$, $A_3$ has $0.00268$, $A_4$ has $0.000257$: about $\frac{1}{10}$ each step.
The eigenvalues are $\frac{5 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2} \approx 4.5616$ and $0.4384$, and $\frac{0.4384}{4.5616} \approx 0.096$. That is the predicted rate.
Meanwhile the diagonal of $A_4$ is $(4.5617, 0.4383)$: the eigenvalues, to about four digits.

blocks.title: Multiplying in the wrong order
blocks.q: What happens if each step forms $Q_kR_k$ instead of $R_kQ_k$?
steps: $Q_kR_k$ is the factorization of $A_k$ itself, so the "new" matrix is $A_k$ again (up to round-off).
Nothing changes, step after step. The reversal of the order is the entire method.

blocks.html: Production codes add three ideas. They first reduce $A$ to Hessenberg form (zeros below the first subdiagonal), which makes each QR step cost $O(n^{2})$ instead of $O(n^{3})$. They use shifts, factoring $A_k - s_kI$ with $s_k$ near an eigenvalue, which turns the slow ratio into a tiny one, just as in Inverse and Shifted Power Methods. And they deflate: once a subdiagonal entry is negligible, the problem splits into smaller ones. All eigenvalues of an $n \times n$ matrix then cost roughly $10n^{3}$ operations.

Multiplying the factors back in the same order, $Q_kR_k$, which just gives $A_k$ again. The step is "factor, then multiply in reverse": $A_{k+1} = R_kQ_k$. Check: the new matrix should differ from the old one but keep the same trace and determinant.
